title: Billing, metering and usage-based pricing
subtitle: Count every unit of usage once, put it in the right billing period, and turn it into an invoice you can prove.

c.v: This story is made up, but each part of it happens. A small company sells an SMS API and charges per message sent.
In March, a network problem slowed the link to the billing service. The API servers retried their usage reports. The
code built each report again, with a new random id each time.
The billing service saw many "new" events. It added them all. Forty customers got invoices for about twice the messages they sent.
A large customer noticed first, because their own logs showed half the number. The team could not show the real count. The monthly job had stored only running totals, not the events behind them.
It took two weeks to rebuild the numbers from server logs. The company refunded everyone. Then it had to answer a harder question: were earlier months wrong too?
, the bill depends on what the customer did: API calls, messages, gigabytes or tokens. So billing is now a counting problem. If you count wrong, you charge wrong.
Counting looks easy. But events get repeated and arrive late. Months start at midnight, but whose midnight? Prices have tiers, and customers change plans mid-month.

Late events and closing a period
An event belongs to the period of its
, not its arrival time. Lago assigns a late event to the right past period by its timestamp. If that period's invoice is already final, the event does not change it.
is the time after a period ends in which late events still count. Stripe's default is 1 hour, and you can set up to 72 hours. It applies to the end-of-cycle invoice, not to threshold invoices.
Stripe accepts event timestamps up to 35 days in the past.
But an accepted event can still miss its invoice. Usage reported after the grace period is not added to the finalized invoice or to the next one.
So decide in advance what happens to very late events. Common choices: bill them as a separate line on the next invoice, or write them off below a set amount. Either way, keep them and count them in
Store every timestamp in UTC. Then define each period boundary as an exact instant.

A customer in India expects "November" to start at 00:00 IST on 1 November. That is 18:30 UTC on 31 October. If your job uses UTC days, five and a half hours of usage land in the wrong month, at both ends of the month. Tools often mean a UTC day by "a day". Stripe's pre-aggregated ingestion keeps only the latest event per UTC hour or day.
Choose the billing timezone per customer, store it, and test the hours around midnight.

q.v: Your service sends a usage event. The request times out, so it retries. Each retry builds the event again with a fresh UUID. What happens?

options.v: Nothing bad. Dedupe catches the retries.
The customer can be billed for the same usage more than once, because each copy has a new id.
The billing system rejects the retries.

why.v: Dedupe only works if a copy has the same id as the original. Create the id once, when the usage happens, and resend the same payload on every retry.

q.v: Graduated price tiers: the first 10,000 calls are free, the next 90,000 cost ₹0.10 each, and every call after 100,000 costs ₹0.05. A customer makes 250,000 calls. What is the charge?
A customer moves from a ₹3,000 plan to a ₹6,000 plan after 10 days of a 30-day month. With proration, what extra amount do they owe for the rest of the month?

why.v: They get a credit of ₹3,000 × 20/30 = ₹2,000 for unused time. They pay ₹6,000 × 20/30 = ₹4,000 for the new plan. The difference is ₹2,000.

q.v: With Stripe Billing meters, a usage event for 30 November arrives after the November invoice has been finalized. What happens to it?

options.v: Stripe adds it to the December invoice.
Stripe can accept it into meter summaries, but it is not added to the finalized invoice or the next one.

why.v: Stripe's docs say usage reported after the grace period is not added to the finalized invoice or to the next invoice. You must handle it yourself.

q.v: You bill for the number of different users who used the product in a month. Which aggregation fits?

why.v: Count unique counts distinct values of a property, such as user id. Sum would count a user once for every event.
